newsitem.title: UK: Premier says oil industry bid wave may slow.
newsitem.headline: Premier says oil industry bid wave may slow.

text.p: Premier Oil Plc said on Monday that the takeover wave rolling through the oil exploration and production industry may slow as shares climbed and opportunities to buy at favourable prices disappeared.

Chief executive Charles Jamieson said Premier itself will likely be less active on the acquisition front than last year when it took over Australia's Discovery Petroleum NL and bought Sumatra Gulf Oil Ltd from Chevron Corp.
"For this year -- although I would not rule out any acquisitions -- our main priority is to get the best out of our portfolio," Jamieson told Reuters.
Premier earlier reported an 80 percent increase in its 1996 net profit to a record 45.3 million stg thanks to higher oil prices and increased production.
Jamieson would not comment on Premier's own chances of remaining independent, but he said business with the group's biggest shareholder -- oil giant Amerada Hess Corp -- continued as usual.

Amerada acquired a 25 percent stake in Premier as the latter bought Pict Petroleum in 1995. Amerada, which has two of its staff on Premier's board, was not allowed to change its holding until mid-February.
Asked whether Premier had been told about any Amerada's plans for its Premier stake, Jamieson said: "We are in fairly continuous contact with them and as far as I can say it's business as usual."
There has been vague speculation Amerada might be interested in raising its stake or even take over Premier, which has promising operations in Burma.
Shares in Premier jumped from levels just over 30 pence late in December to a peak of 43 pence on January 17. They traded 1/2 penny higher at 38 this morning.

Fuelled by a flurry of takeovers and announcements on new finds, shares in oil exploration and production firms were the star performers last year. But this may have dampened further bid activity, Jamieson said.
"Share prices have certainly risen, so there doesn't look to be quite the discrepancy in values that used to be around. It might just slow down," he said.
Premier said cash flow per share rose to 6.1 pence per share from 3.9 pence in 1995, while reserves per share were up at 0.19 barrel of oil equivalent from 0.16.
Despite the strong performance last year, Jamieson said Premier was not bringing forward its goal to double the 1995 cash flow and reserve per share figures by next year
"We are still working on end-1998," he said.
Daily production rose to around 45,000 barrels of oil equivalent in 1996 from an average 32,000 the previous year.
"We expect that (production) to be sustained during 1997, which would give us strong cash flow for the year," he said.

Premier's exploration programme this year includes 25 to 30 wells in about eight countries. One of its main projects for 1997 is to prove more reserves at the major Yetagun gas field offshore Burma to sell more gas to Thailand.
Texaco Inc operates the Yetagun field, in which it has a 50 percent interest, Premier holds 30 percent and Nippon Oil the remaining 20 percent. Commercial production is set to start in 1999.
Premier's exploration project in the south of Albania, which employs a total of 25 staff, was not affected by the armed revolt in the Balkan state.
The Patoz Marinze oil field is located at about a three hours drive north of the southern town of Vlore, where the revolt started.
"None of this unrest is directed towards Premier or other foreign companies," Jamieson said, adding measures to ensure safety of the staff had been taken.
